videos.title: NEC Talks: AI-assisted Multimodal Scientific Content Generation
videos.description:
Prof. Dr. Steffen Eger, Full Professor at the University of Technology Nuremberg (UTN)
Christian Greisinger, PhD student at the University of Technology Nuremberg (UTN)

Abstract:
AI4Science approaches that aid scientists in scientific content production, accelerating the pace of research, are recently gaining considerable momentum and promise to revolutionize the scientific workflow. In this talk, after giving a brief high-level overview over different AI4Science tasks considered in our recent ACM Computing Survey paper and EACL tutorial, including AI-assisted literature search and AI-assisted reviewing, we will cover our recent progress in multimodal scientific content generation for science. In particular, we will discuss datasets and modeling approaches for scientific figure generation from captions, textual descriptions or sketches using TikZ as a coding language. We will also present our ongoing works in this direction, targeted at automatically editing scientific figures and at leveraging multiple coding languages (Python, TikZ, …) for more adequate content generation. We will outline the challenges and opportunities of the approaches and the promise they hold for enabling efficient, high-quality multimodal scientific content generation, additionally aimed at fostering diversity and inclusivity.  

About the speakers:
Since 2024, Steffen Eger is Full Professor at the University of Technology Nuremberg (UTN), leading the Natural Language Learning and Generation (NLLG) lab. His research targets diverse problems at the intersection of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Artificial Intelligence, the humanities and social sciences. Recent focus areas include evaluation of generative AI (e.g., machine translation, text-to-image generation), machine translation for literature, multimodal AI4Science applications, diachronic text analysis (e.g. how biases/solidarity change over time) and authorship and argumentation mining applications, among others.  

Since 2025, Christian Greisinger has been a PhD student at UTN and a member of the NLLG Lab. Under the supervision of Prof. Dr. Steffen Eger, his research focuses on multimodal content generation for AI in science. In particular, he investigates how smaller open-source models can be improved to achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art proprietary systems while remaining more efficient and cost-effective. His recent research on Text-to-TikZ generation was accepted at ICLR 2026, and he is currently exploring the transfer of these methods to scientific image editing.

videos.title: What is SigLIP?
videos.description:
What is SigLIP?
SigLIP swaps CLIP's batch-wide softmax for a simple pairwise sigmoid loss, so image-text pretraining scales cleanly and gets stronger zero-shot.

If you have used a modern vision-language model, there is a good chance an encoder like this is quietly doing the heavy lifting. SigLIP, from Zhai and colleagues at Google in twenty twenty-three, trains an image encoder and a text encoder to agree with each other, much like CLIP does. Feed it a picture and a caption, and it learns to place matching pairs close together in a shared space. But it changes one thing that turns out to matter a lot. The loss function. And that single swap makes it simpler, cheaper, and stronger. Today we unpack why that tiny change ripples all the way out to how you train and how well the model classifies.

videos.title: CLAP: Direct VLM-to-VLA Robot Adaptation
videos.description: In this AI Research Roundup episode, Alex discusses the paper: 'CLAP: Direct VLM-to-VLA Adaptation via Language-Action Grounding' This paper introduces CLAP (Causal Language-Action Prediction), a method to directly convert pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) with minimal architectural changes. Typically, adapting VLMs to robotics causes output-distribution mismatch because numeric action tokens deviate from natural language. CLAP solves this by prepending numeric action sequences with natural-language action descriptions, conditioning the model on a language-action plan. With single-epoch fine-tuning, CLAP achieves 90.8% on the LIBERO benchmark and shows high robustness against spatial and language perturbations. The researchers have released CLAP as an open-weight, multi-scale compact VLA family to help study VLM-to-VLA capability transfer.
